setting: A short campus sustainability talk about keeping bees in cities and how it relates to local food.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk at a campus sustainability event.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: When people picture beekeeping, they often imagine quiet countryside farms.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: But a growing number of cities now host rooftop and community-garden hives.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Urban bees can forage on parks, balconies, and street trees—sometimes finding a surprising variety of flowers.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Local honey is one product, yet the bigger story is pollination for neighborhood gardens and small farms at the city edge.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Beekeepers must follow city rules: hive registration, safe distances from sidewalks, and water sources so bees do not crowd fountains.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Neighbors worry about stings, so responsible keepers post signs and choose gentle bee strains.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Pesticides remain a challenge; some cities limit spraying during bloom periods to protect pollinators.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Students here can volunteer with the campus apiary and track bloom calendars for the gardens.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: The point is not that every resident should keep bees—it is that pollinators are part of a healthier local food system.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next month's workshop will cover how to plant a pollinator strip with native flowers.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How to cook with honey in a dorm kitchen
options.B: Urban beekeeping and its link to local food and pollination
options.C: Why cities should ban all insects
options.D: How to build a wooden fence for a farm

questions.explanation: The speaker explains city hives, pollination, rules, and why pollinators support local food systems.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—honey is mentioned as one product, not the main focus.

questions.narrator_text: According to the speaker, what is the bigger story beyond local honey?

options.B: Pollination for neighborhood gardens and small farms at the city edge

questions.explanation: He says the bigger story is pollination for neighborhood gardens and small farms at the city edge.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A or D—those are not mentioned.

questions.narrator_text: What city rules for beekeepers does he mention?

options.A: Hive registration, safe distances from sidewalks, and water sources
options.B: A requirement to keep bees only indoors
options.C: A ban on all community gardens
options.D: Mandatory daily spraying of every flower

questions.explanation: Keepers must follow registration, safe distances from sidewalks, and provide water sources.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing D—he says pesticides are a challenge and some cities limit spraying.

questions.narrator_text: What does the speaker suggest about who should keep bees?

options.A: Every resident must keep a hive
options.B: Not everyone needs to keep bees; pollinators still matter for local food systems
options.D: Beekeeping has no connection to food

questions.explanation: He says the point is not that every resident should keep bees, but that pollinators are part of a healthier local food system.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—that is what he explicitly rejects.
